title: AIIMS NORCET FON Pattern Full Test (100 Questions) — ADPIE, Priority, Communication & Ethics
description: 100-question AIIMS NORCET Prelims pattern mock test covering Nursing Process (ADPIE), Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow), Communication in Nursing, and Ethics & Legal Issues with +1/-0.33 marking, MSQs, and full explanations.
subject: norcet-fon
instructions: AIIMS NORCET Prelims Pattern — Fundamentals of Nursing (100 Questions / 90 Minutes)
Sections: ADPIE (25Q), Priority Settings ABC & Maslow (25Q), Communication (25Q), Ethics & Legal Issues (25Q)
Marking Scheme: +1 mark per correct response | -0.33 negative mark per wrong attempt | 0 for skipped
Hint Coins: 5 Hint Coins credited (5% of 100 questions) — hints stay disabled until clicked

questions.question: A nurse admits a 72-year-old patient with heart failure who reports orthopnea and ankle swelling. After auscultating bibasilar crackles and checking a BNP level of 940 pg/mL, the nurse groups these findings together to identify a pattern. Which sub-step of the assessment phase is the nurse performing?

options.text: Data validation
Cue clustering (data organization)
Outcome evaluation
Intervention delegation

questions.explanation: Cue clustering involves grouping related subjective and objective assessment cues (orthopnea, edema, crackles, elevated BNP) to recognize clinical patterns that lead to an accurate nursing diagnosis (e.g., Excess Fluid Volume).
questions.hint: Think about the step that organizes scattered clinical signs into a meaningful pattern before naming a diagnosis.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: A newly graduated nurse records a patient's blood pressure as 188/110 mmHg using an automatic cuff, even though the patient's baseline is 118/74 mmHg and the patient feels completely asymptomatic. What is the nurse's MOST appropriate next step in the assessment phase?

options.text: Immediately formulate a nursing diagnosis of ineffective tissue perfusion
Validate the reading by rechecking manually with an appropriately sized cuff on the opposite arm
Document the reading and ignore it since the patient is asymptomatic
Administer an extra dose of antihypertensive medication without verifying

questions.explanation: Data validation (double-checking) is essential whenever subjective and objective data conflict or a reading deviates sharply from baseline. Using the wrong cuff size or faulty equipment can cause false hypertension readings.
questions.hint: Before acting on an unexpected outlying measurement, consider how to ensure the data itself is accurate.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: Which of the following are valid types of NANDA-I nursing diagnoses? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Problem-focused (actual) nursing diagnosis
Risk nursing diagnosis
Health promotion nursing diagnosis
Pathophysiological medical diagnosis

questions.explanation: NANDA-I recognizes problem-focused (actual), risk, health promotion, and syndrome nursing diagnoses. Pathophysiological disease labels (e.g., diabetes mellitus) are medical diagnoses, not nursing diagnoses.
questions.hint: Identify the three categories recognized by NANDA-I taxonomy and exclude medical disease terminology.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: A healthy 32-year-old pregnant woman tells the antenatal clinic nurse, "I want to learn healthy meal planning and safe exercises for my second trimester." Which type of NANDA-I nursing diagnosis is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Risk nursing diagnosis
Problem-focused nursing diagnosis
Health promotion nursing diagnosis
Syndrome nursing diagnosis

questions.explanation: A health promotion nursing diagnosis ("Readiness for enhanced nutrition" or "Readiness for enhanced health management") applies when a patient expresses motivation and desire to increase well-being and actualize health potential.
questions.hint: Focus on the patient's expressed desire to improve an already healthy state rather than treating a deficit.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: A nurse is reviewing a student's care plan and sees the nursing diagnosis: "Impaired physical mobility related to fractured femur as evidenced by inability to bear weight." What error did the student make in writing the etiology?

options.text: The student used an incorrect problem label
The student used a medical diagnosis ("fractured femur") as the etiology instead of a modifiable nursing factor
The student omitted defining characteristics
The student used a risk diagnosis format

questions.explanation: In a NANDA-I statement, the etiology ("related to") should identify factors that nursing interventions can modify (e.g., pain, musculoskeletal impairment, prescribed activity restriction), rather than a fixed medical diagnosis ("fractured femur") that nurses cannot directly treat.
questions.hint: Check whether the "related to" clause describes something nursing care can directly modify or a medical condition.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: A nurse is preparing a care plan for a patient with chronic kidney disease using the Nursing Outcomes Classification (NOC) and Nursing Interventions Classification (NIC). Which ADPIE phases do NOC and NIC correspond to respectively?

options.text: Assessment and Diagnosis
Planning (expected outcomes) and Implementation/Planning (interventions)
Diagnosis and Evaluation only
Implementation and Assessment

questions.explanation: NANDA-I standardizes Nursing Diagnoses, NOC (Nursing Outcomes Classification) standardizes measurable patient outcomes in the Planning/Evaluation phases, and NIC (Nursing Interventions Classification) standardizes nursing actions for Implementation.
questions.hint: Match "Outcomes" and "Interventions" to their corresponding steps in ADPIE.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: A nurse is writing a short-term goal for a postoperative abdominal surgery patient on day 1. Which goal is BEST classified as a short-term goal?

options.text: The patient will return to full-time office work within 6 weeks
The patient will lose 10 kg over the next 6 months
The patient will demonstrate effective incentive spirometry use (10 breaths/hour) within 4 hours
The patient will remain smoke-free for 1 year after discharge

questions.explanation: Short-term goals are achieved within hours to a few days (typically < 1 week) and address immediate inpatient recovery needs. Long-term goals span weeks or months for rehabilitation or lifestyle change.
questions.hint: Compare the timeframe of each goal to identify which one is achievable within the same shift or day.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: During the implementation phase, a nurse administers prescribed IV vancomycin and monitors peak and trough drug levels in coordination with the clinical pharmacist. How are these two actions classified respectively?

options.text: Both are independent nursing interventions
Administering prescribed IV vancomycin is dependent; coordinating drug levels with the pharmacist is collaborative
Both are collaborative interventions
Administering vancomycin is collaborative; consulting the pharmacist is independent

questions.explanation: Dependent interventions require a physician's order (administering prescription drugs). Collaborative (interdependent) interventions involve joint care with other healthcare disciplines (pharmacist, physiotherapist, dietitian).
questions.hint: Separate an action strictly triggered by a doctor's order from one involving multidisciplinary teamwork.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: Before implementing a physician's order for a 10x higher-than-usual dose of morphine, what is the nurse's legal and professional duty during the implementation phase of ADPIE?

options.text: Administer the dose as written because it is a dependent intervention
Question and clarify the order with the prescribing physician before administering the drug
Administer half the dose without informing anyone
Ask a nursing assistant to give the medication instead

questions.explanation: Implementation is never blind execution. Nurses are legally accountable for reassessing safety before every intervention and must clarify or refuse potentially harmful orders.
questions.hint: Recall a nurse's independent duty of clinical judgment even when carrying out a physician's prescription.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: A nurse documents a patient's progress note using the DAR format: Data, Action, Response. Which charting system is the nurse utilizing?

options.text: Problem-Oriented Medical Record (SOAP)
Focus Charting
Charting by Exception (CBE)
Narrative Chronological Charting

questions.explanation: Focus Charting organizes documentation around a patient-centered "Focus" (concern, behavior, or event) using the DAR structure: Data (subjective/objective), Action (nursing interventions), and Response (patient evaluation).
questions.hint: Link the three-letter DAR acronym to the charting model centered on a specific patient "focus."
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: Which nursing actions are required during the Evaluation phase of ADPIE? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Comparing actual patient outcomes with pre-established expected outcome criteria
Determining whether the care plan should be continued, modified, or terminated
Skipping reassessment if the intervention was completed on time
Identifying factors that facilitated or hindered goal achievement

questions.explanation: Evaluation requires comparing observed data against expected outcomes, analyzing why goals were or were not met, and deciding whether to continue, modify, or discontinue the care plan.
questions.hint: Think about all the analytical steps needed to judge whether nursing care actually worked.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: A nurse performs a comprehensive health history and head-to-toe examination within 24 hours of a patient's admission to a medical ward. Three months later, at a follow-up outpatient visit, the nurse compares the patient's current HbA1c and foot health against baseline data. What are these two assessments called respectively?

options.text: Initial assessment and time-lapsed assessment
Emergency assessment and focused assessment
Focused assessment and initial assessment
Time-lapsed assessment and emergency assessment

questions.explanation: An initial (comprehensive) assessment establishes a complete baseline at admission. A time-lapsed assessment occurs weeks or months later to compare current status with previously obtained baseline data.
questions.hint: Contrast a first-time admission baseline with a periodic comparison done months later.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: A nurse uses Gordon's Functional Health Patterns during an admission interview. What is the primary purpose of using this framework in the nursing process?

options.text: To calculate hospital billing codes
To systematically organize holistic assessment data across 11 functional health domains
To replace physician physical examinations
To determine nurse-to-patient staffing ratios

questions.explanation: Marjory Gordon's 11 Functional Health Patterns (e.g., Health Perception, Nutritional-Metabolic, Elimination, Activity-Exercise, Sleep-Rest, Cognitive-Perceptual, Coping-Stress) provide a structured nursing framework for holistic assessment.
questions.hint: Recall what Marjory Gordon's 11-pattern model helps nurses organize during data collection.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: Which statement about the Kardex system in nursing care planning is TRUE?

options.text: It is a permanent legal part of the patient's archived medical record
It is a quick-reference, portable summary of current orders, allergies, diet, and nursing care plans updated continuously
It is used solely for documenting narcotic wastage
It replaces the need for nursing progress notes

questions.explanation: The Kardex (card file or electronic summary) provides a concise, up-to-date bedside reference of key care details (allergies, IVs, diet, activity, treatments) for shift handoffs, though it is generally a working tool rather than a permanent legal record.
questions.hint: Think of the concise working reference tool nurses consult at shift change for active orders and care summaries.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: A nurse is delegating tasks to a Licensed Practical Nurse (LPN / GNM junior staff under supervision in mixed staffing) and a UAP. Which of the Five Rights of Delegation ensures that the delegatee actually has the knowledge and skill to perform the task safely?

options.text: Right Task
Right Circumstance
Right Person
Right Direction and Communication

questions.explanation: The Five Rights of Delegation (NCSBN/ANA) are: Right Task, Right Circumstance, Right Person (verifying competency and scope of practice), Right Direction/Communication, and Right Supervision/Evaluation.
questions.hint: Match verifying an individual's competence and scope of practice to one of the Five Rights.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: During a physical assessment, a nurse taps directly on a patient's chest wall using the middle finger of the dominant hand against the middle finger of the non-dominant hand placed flat on the skin. Which technique is being used, and what sound is expected over healthy lung tissue?

options.text: Direct percussion; dullness
Indirect (mediate) percussion; resonance
Palpation; tympany
Auscultation; vesicular

questions.explanation: Indirect (mediate) percussion uses a pleximeter finger (on skin) struck by a plexor finger. Normal air-filled lung parenchyma produces a low-pitched, hollow sound called resonance.
questions.hint: Recall the two-handed tapping technique and the normal acoustic sound over aerated lungs.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: A patient with pneumonia has the nursing diagnosis "Ineffective airway clearance related to retained tracheobronchial secretions." Which finding during the evaluation phase BEST indicates that nursing interventions were effective?

options.text: The patient drank 200 mL of water
Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally and SpO2 improved from 89% to 97% on room air
The nurse performed chest physiotherapy three times
The patient's family understands the discharge instructions

questions.explanation: Evaluation must measure objective patient outcomes directly linked to the diagnosis (airway clearance -> clear breath sounds and improved oxygenation), not merely whether the nurse performed the task.
questions.hint: Look for objective clinical proof that the patient's airways are actually clear.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a SYNDROME nursing diagnosis according to NANDA-I?

options.text: Impaired urinary elimination
Risk for infection
Rape-trauma syndrome (or Relocation stress syndrome / Chronic pain syndrome)
Readiness for enhanced coping

questions.explanation: A syndrome nursing diagnosis comprises a cluster of actual or risk nursing diagnoses predicted to occur together because of a specific event or situation (e.g., Rape-trauma syndrome, Frail elderly syndrome, Relocation stress syndrome).
questions.hint: Identify the diagnosis representing a predictable cluster of multiple nursing problems triggered by one major event.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: A nurse uses "Charting by Exception" (CBE) on an ICU ward. What is the fundamental principle of CBE?

options.text: Writing long narrative paragraphs every 2 hours
Documenting only significant abnormal findings or deviations from pre-established normal standards
Omitting vital signs from the medical record
Recording nursing diagnoses without interventions

questions.explanation: Charting by Exception (CBE) uses standardized flow sheets and protocols where only abnormal findings or exceptions to defined norms require narrative documentation, reducing repetitive charting.
questions.hint: Let the word "exception" guide you to what gets detailed narrative entries in this system.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: While conducting a focused respiratory assessment on a patient admitted for acute asthma, the nurse notes wheezing, tachypnea (28/min), and pursed-lip breathing. What makes this a "focused" assessment rather than an "initial" assessment?

options.text: It is only done by physicians
It concentrates specifically on one body system or acute problem rather than a complete head-to-toe database
It does not include objective data
It is performed only at discharge

questions.explanation: A focused (problem-focused) assessment gathers targeted data about a specific existing health problem or body system to monitor status or evaluate response to treatment.
questions.hint: Contrast examining one symptomatic body system against doing a full head-to-toe baseline.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Nursing diagnoses change dynamically as the patient's physiological and psychosocial responses evolve.
Reason (R): A nursing diagnosis is based on a permanent pathological disease entity identified by laboratory testing alone.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.explanation: Nursing diagnoses evolve as the patient improves or develops new responses (A is true). Medical diagnoses—not nursing diagnoses—are based on pathological disease entities (R is false).
questions.hint: Evaluate whether Reason (R) describes a nursing diagnosis or a medical diagnosis.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: A nurse observes a patient clutching their abdomen and grimacing, yet when asked, the patient states, "I have no pain at all." What is the nurse's MOST appropriate action in the assessment phase?

options.text: Document "no pain" and move on
Clarify the discrepancy between the verbal report and non-verbal cues using empathetic inquiry
Administer IV opioids immediately without asking further
Ignore the grimacing because subjective data always overrides observation

questions.explanation: When subjective verbal reports conflict with objective non-verbal cues (guarding, grimacing), the nurse must validate and explore the inconsistency—the patient may fear addiction, want to appear stoic, or worry about delaying discharge.
questions.hint: Think about how a nurse reconciles conflicting verbal and non-verbal assessment cues.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: Which of the following are essential components of the Planning phase of ADPIE? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Setting clinical priorities among identified nursing diagnoses
Establishing measurable, patient-centered SMART goals and expected outcomes
Selecting evidence-based nursing interventions tailored to the patient
Performing the initial head-to-toe physical examination

questions.explanation: The Planning phase includes prioritizing diagnoses, writing SMART goals/outcomes, selecting nursing interventions, and writing/updating the individualized care plan. Physical examination belongs to Assessment.
questions.hint: Separate care-plan design activities from initial data collection.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: A nurse is evaluating a diabetic patient's discharge teaching by asking the patient to explain how to recognize and treat hypoglycemia in their own words. Which evaluation technique is the nurse using?

options.text: Charting by Exception
Teach-back method
SBAR handoff
Indirect percussion

questions.explanation: The teach-back method asks patients to explain or demonstrate key instructions in their own words to verify comprehension during the evaluation phase of patient education.
questions.hint: Name the patient-education verification technique where the patient "teaches" the concept back to the nurse.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: Which sequence correctly represents the five cyclical steps of the Nursing Process (ADPIE)?

options.text: Assessment -> Planning -> Diagnosis -> Implementation -> Evaluation
Assessment -> Diagnosis -> Planning -> Implementation -> Evaluation
Diagnosis -> Assessment -> Planning -> Evaluation -> Implementation
Assessment -> Diagnosis -> Implementation -> Planning -> Evaluation

questions.explanation: ADPIE stands for Assessment, Diagnosis, Planning, Implementation, and Evaluation. Each step builds logically on the previous one while remaining dynamic and cyclical.
questions.hint: Spell out the standard five-letter mnemonic used worldwide for the nursing process.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: Four patients arrive simultaneously at the emergency triage desk. Using the ABC framework, which patient should the triage nurse prioritize FIRST?

options.text: A 40-year-old with a deep forearm laceration bleeding slowly and BP 122/78 mmHg
A 28-year-old with facial burns, singed nasal hairs, and carbonaceous sputum
A 55-year-old with a deformed right ankle rating pain at 9/10
A 62-year-old with a blood glucose of 290 mg/dL and normal breathing

questions.explanation: Facial burns, singed nasal hairs, and carbonaceous sputum indicate inhalation injury with imminent risk of rapid upper-airway edema and obstruction (Airway emergency), outranking bleeding control, extremity pain, or uncomplicated hyperglycemia.
questions.hint: Look for classic red-flag signs of impending upper-airway obstruction from thermal injury.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A nurse is caring for four patients on a surgical ward. Which patient should the nurse see FIRST after receiving morning shift report?

options.text: A patient 2 days post-cholecystectomy requesting oral acetaminophen for 4/10 pain
A patient with a urinary catheter whose output was 120 mL over the past 3 hours
A patient 4 hours post-abdominal surgery whose surgical dressing is soaked with bright red blood and whose HR increased from 82 to 124/min
A patient scheduled for discharge at noon waiting for wound care pamphlets

questions.explanation: Bright red saturated dressing with new tachycardia indicates active postoperative hemorrhage (Circulation instability / acute unexpected change), taking top priority over expected pain, adequate urine output (40 mL/hr), or routine discharge.
questions.hint: Identify the patient showing acute hemodynamic instability from active blood loss.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question:
According to Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs, arrange the following patient needs from HIGHEST priority (1) to LOWEST priority (4):
1. Preventing falls in an unsteady patient
2. Treating acute hypoxia (SpO2 85%)
3. Encouraging family visits to reduce loneliness
4. Supporting a patient's desire to achieve personal recovery milestones
questions.explanation: Maslow's order from base (highest priority) upward is: Physiological (hypoxia = 2) -> Safety & Security (fall prevention = 1) -> Love & Belonging (family visits = 3) -> Self-Esteem / Self-Actualization (personal milestones = 4).
questions.hint: Place survival/oxygenation at the very bottom, followed by physical safety, social connection, and personal growth.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A patient with a tracheostomy accidentally decannulates (the tube falls out completely) 24 hours after insertion, and the patient becomes severely dyspneic and cyanotic. What is the nurse's FIRST priority action?

options.text: Leave the room to fetch a new tracheostomy kit from the supply room
Stay with the patient, call for immediate emergency help, and maintain airway patency using a tracheal dilator/obtulator or bag-valve-mask oxygenation per protocol
Document the decannulation time in the chart first
Place the patient flat in supine position without oxygen

questions.explanation: Accidental decannulation within the first 72 hours (before the stoma tract matures) is an acute Airway emergency. The nurse must never leave the patient; call for help immediately while maintaining airway patency and oxygenation.
questions.hint: Apply the Airway-first rule and remember never to abandon a patient in acute airway collapse.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A nurse receives critical laboratory values for four different patients at the same time. Which value requires the MOST urgent intervention?

options.text: Hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL in a chronic kidney disease patient
Blood glucose 210 mg/dL in a patient with Type 2 diabetes
Serum potassium 6.9 mEq/L with peaked T waves on the cardiac monitor
White blood cell count 12,500/mm3 in a patient receiving IV antibiotics for cellulitis

questions.explanation: Severe hyperkalemia (6.9 mEq/L) with ECG changes (peaked T waves) poses an immediate risk of lethal ventricular fibrillation or cardiac arrest (Circulation emergency). The other labs are chronic or non-immediately life-threatening.
questions.hint: Identify the electrolyte abnormality that can cause sudden lethal cardiac arrest within minutes.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: Which situations require the nurse to INTERVENE IMMEDIATELY rather than performing an extended assessment first? (Select all that apply)

options.text: A patient's arterial line disconnects and bright red blood is spurting onto the bed
A patient is actively choking with silent cough and universal choking sign
A patient reports mild nausea 1 hour after breakfast
A patient is found unresponsive without breathing or pulse

questions.explanation: While ADPIE generally starts with assessment, immediate life-threatening ABC/CAB emergencies (arterial hemorrhage, complete airway obstruction, cardiac arrest) require instant life-saving intervention.
questions.hint: Look for scenarios where delaying even 30 seconds for a lengthy assessment could be fatal.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A nurse is prioritizing care for a patient with acute bacterial meningitis who has a fever of 39.8 C, nuchal rigidity, photophobia, and sudden onset of new confusion and lethargy. Which nursing concern takes the HIGHEST priority?

options.text: Dimming the room lights for photophobia
Monitoring airway, neurological status (ICP/GCS), and initiating prescribed IV antibiotics promptly
Providing a warm bath for comfort
Teaching family members about vaccination schedules

questions.explanation: New confusion and lethargy in meningitis signal increasing intracranial pressure (ICP) and risk of airway compromise or herniation. Protecting airway/neurological stability and rapid antimicrobial therapy outrank comfort or education.
questions.hint: Focus on signs of worsening cerebral perfusion and potential airway loss over comfort measures.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A patient with congestive heart failure receiving IV furosemide develops pink, frothy sputum, severe dyspnea, and crackles throughout all lung fields. What is the nurse's FIRST bedside action?

options.text: Administer an oral cough suppressant
Place the patient in High-Fowler's position with legs dependent and apply prescribed high-flow oxygen
Encourage the patient to drink 500 mL of water to thin secretions
Obtain a routine 24-hour dietary recall

questions.explanation: Pink frothy sputum with diffuse crackles indicates acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema (flash pulmonary edema)—a Breathing/Circulation emergency. High-Fowler's with legs dangling decreases venous return (preload), and oxygen addresses acute hypoxemia.
questions.hint: Think of the immediate bedside positioning and oxygenation steps that reduce lung congestion and preload.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: In the clinical prioritization rule "Actual vs. Potential Problems," which nursing diagnosis should the nurse address FIRST?

options.text: Risk for falls related to antihypertensive therapy
Risk for constipation related to opioid analgesics
Fluid volume deficit related to severe vomiting and diarrhea as evidenced by BP 86/54 mmHg and oliguria
Risk for social isolation related to contact precautions

questions.explanation: An actual physiological problem causing active hemodynamic instability (Fluid volume deficit with hypotension and oliguria) always outranks potential ("Risk for...") diagnoses.
questions.hint: Separate a currently occurring hemodynamic crisis from future preventive risks.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a patient with a new plaster cast on the right forearm who reports severe, escalating pain unrelieved by IV morphine, along with paresthesia and pale, cool fingers. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.text: Elevate the arm high above heart level and apply ice tightly
Reassure the patient that cast pain is normal and recheck in 4 hours
Notify the physician immediately for suspected acute compartment syndrome and prepare for cast bivalving
Administer another dose of oral ibuprofen and document

questions.explanation: Severe unrelieved pain, paresthesia, pallor, and coolness are classic signs of acute compartment syndrome (threat to peripheral Circulation/limb viability). Immediate provider notification for cast splitting/bivalving is urgent; high elevation above the heart worsens arterial ischemia.
questions.hint: Recognize the surgical limb-threatening emergency characterized by escalating pain unrelieved by opioids.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A psychiatric patient on an inpatient ward expresses active suicidal ideation with a specific plan to hang themselves tonight. Using Maslow's Hierarchy, which need is the nurse prioritizing by placing the patient on 1:1 continuous observation and removing ligature hazards?

options.text: Self-actualization
Love and belonging
Safety and security (physical safety)
Self-esteem

questions.explanation: Protecting a patient from imminent self-harm directly addresses physical Safety and Security—the highest priority once immediate physiological airway/breathing/circulation stability is intact.
questions.hint: Match suicide precautions and hazard removal to the corresponding tier of Maslow's pyramid.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: During a ward fire (RACE protocol), a nurse discovers smoke pouring from an unoccupied utility closet next to a bedridden patient's room. What is the nurse's FIRST priority action?

options.text: Extinguish the fire using a fire extinguisher
Rescue/remove the patient from immediate danger
Close all windows and doors on the ward
Write an incident report for hospital administration

questions.explanation: The RACE fire safety priority sequence is: Rescue (remove patients in immediate danger), Alarm (activate fire alarm/call code red), Confine (close doors/windows), and Extinguish/Evacuate.
questions.hint: Recall the first letter of the hospital fire-response acronym RACE.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A nurse is assessing four patients on a postpartum unit. Which patient should be assessed FIRST?

options.text: A woman 12 hours postpartum with a firm fundus at the umbilicus and moderate lochia rubra
A woman 24 hours postpartum asking for help with breastfeeding latch
A woman 2 hours postpartum with a boggy, deviated uterus and two perineal pads saturated within 30 minutes
A woman 36 hours postpartum reporting mild afterpains during nursing

questions.explanation: A boggy uterus with rapid saturation of perineal pads indicates uterine atony and postpartum hemorrhage (PPH)—an acute Circulation emergency requiring immediate fundal massage and intervention.
questions.hint: Identify the unexpected sign of active postpartum hemorrhage versus normal involution findings.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A nurse is prioritizing interventions for a patient admitted with hypothermia (core body temperature 31.5 C), bradycardia (46/min), and lethargy. Which principle guides the nurse to address core rewarming and cardiac monitoring BEFORE conducting a family psychosocial history?

options.text: Psychosocial needs take precedence over thermoregulation
Physiological needs (thermoregulation and cardiac stability) in Maslow's hierarchy take precedence over psychosocial needs
Chronic needs take precedence over acute needs
Least invasive interventions are always skipped in hypothermia

questions.explanation: Severe hypothermia threatens core physiological stability and carries high risk of ventricular fibrillation. Physiological survival needs (Maslow's base + Circulation) always precede psychosocial history.
questions.hint: Apply Maslow's base tier to severe thermoregulatory and cardiac instability.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: Which patient findings indicate an UNSTABLE clinical status requiring immediate priority over stable patients? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Sudden drop in Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score from 15 to 10
New-onset chest pain radiating to the left jaw with diaphoresis
Chronic blood pressure of 136/84 mmHg in a patient with longstanding controlled hypertension
Postoperative urine output of 10 mL over the past 2 hours

questions.explanation: Acute neurological decline (GCS drop), suspected acute coronary syndrome, and acute oliguria (< 30 mL/hr) represent unstable, acute physiological deterioration. Stable mild chronic hypertension is low priority.
questions.hint: Select the three acute physiological deteriorations and leave out the stable chronic baseline.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A patient receiving a packed red blood cell (PRBC) transfusion develops chills, fever of 39.2 C, flank pain, and hypotension 15 minutes into the infusion. What is the nurse's FIRST priority action?

options.text: Stop the blood transfusion immediately and keep the IV line patent with normal saline using new tubing
Slow the transfusion rate by half and administer antipyretics
Wait 30 minutes to see if symptoms resolve spontaneously
Flush the existing blood tubing with dextrose 5% in water

questions.explanation: Chills, fever, flank pain, and hypotension signal an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction (life-threatening Circulation/renal emergency). Stopping the transfusion immediately prevents further hemolysis; never flush the blood remaining in the tubing into the patient.
questions.hint: Think of the very first step to halt exposure to an incompatible blood product.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: When applying the ABCDE trauma primary survey to a road traffic accident victim in the emergency department, what does "D" stand for?

options.text: Diet and hydration
Disability (brief neurological assessment: AVPU/GCS and pupils)
Discharge planning
Dressing of minor abrasions

questions.explanation: In the ATLS/trauma primary survey, ABCDE stands for: Airway (with cervical spine protection), Breathing, Circulation (with hemorrhage control), Disability (neurological status), and Exposure/Environmental control.
questions.hint: Recall what rapid neurological check immediately follows Airway, Breathing, and Circulation in trauma care.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a patient with myasthenia gravis who reports increasing difficulty swallowing saliva, weak cough, and shallow respirations (RR 30/min). Which nursing diagnosis takes the HIGHEST priority?

options.text: Imbalanced nutrition: less than body requirements
Impaired verbal communication
Ineffective breathing pattern / Risk for aspiration (airway and breathing compromise)
Activity intolerance

questions.explanation: Bulbar muscle weakness and shallow tachypnea signal impending myasthenic crisis with respiratory failure and aspiration risk—an Airway and Breathing emergency.
questions.hint: Prioritize the respiratory muscle weakness threatening ventilation and airway protection.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A patient with severe sepsis has a serum lactate of 5.2 mmol/L, MAP of 56 mmHg, and warm flushed skin. Which priority framework justifies rapid IV crystalloid resuscitation and broad-spectrum antibiotics within the first hour?

options.text: Love and belonging tier of Maslow's hierarchy
Circulation/Perfusion priority under ABC (and Surviving Sepsis 1-hour bundle)
Self-esteem preservation framework
Chronic disease rehabilitation model

questions.explanation: Septic shock causes severe vasodilation and tissue hypoperfusion (MAP < 65 mmHg, elevated lactate). Restoring circulation/perfusion and treating the infectious source within the 1-hour bundle directly addresses the Circulation priority.
questions.hint: Link low mean arterial pressure and elevated lactate to the specific component of ABC that is failing.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A nurse on a pediatric ward has four patients. Which child should the nurse assess FIRST?

options.text: A 6-year-old with a casted arm watching cartoons comfortably
A 4-year-old with mild viral gastroenteritis tolerating oral rehydration sips
A 3-year-old with suspected acute epiglottitis sitting upright in tripod position, drooling, with inspiratory stridor
An 8-year-old scheduled for routine discharge teaching on asthma inhaler use

questions.explanation: Tripod positioning, drooling, and inspiratory stridor are classic signs of acute epiglottitis—a life-threatening Airway emergency (never inspect the throat with a tongue depressor as it may trigger complete laryngospasm).
questions.hint: Identify the pediatric airway emergency presenting with drooling and tripod posture.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: When choosing between two interventions for a patient with mild postoperative anxiety and a stable SpO2 of 98%, which clinical prioritization principle supports trying deep-breathing relaxation techniques before requesting a PRN sedative injection?

options.text: Most invasive intervention first
Least restrictive / least invasive intervention first
Dependent intervention before independent intervention
Potential risk before actual crisis

questions.explanation: When a patient is physiologically stable, nursing prioritization favors the least invasive, least restrictive safe intervention (independent non-pharmacological measures) before escalating to medications or restraints.
questions.hint: Consider the safety principle that prefers non-pharmacological, non-invasive measures when the patient is stable.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A patient in the ICU has an intracranial pressure (ICP) monitor reading 26 mmHg (normal 5–15 mmHg), bradycardia (48/min), widening pulse pressure (170/68 mmHg), and irregular respirations. What does this triad indicate, and what is its priority level?

options.text: Normal sleep response; low priority
Cushing's triad indicating impending brainstem herniation; immediate life-threatening emergency
Orthostatic hypotension; moderate priority
Expected response to analgesics; routine priority

questions.explanation: Cushing's triad (hypertension with widening pulse pressure, bradycardia, and irregular respirations) is a late, critical sign of severely increased ICP and impending brain herniation requiring immediate emergency intervention.
questions.hint: Recognize the classic three-sign triad signaling critical intracranial hypertension.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a patient with acute pain (8/10) from a renal stone and another patient whose IV site shows mild redness without swelling, alongside a third patient with acute hypoxia (SpO2 82%). In what order should the nurse attend to these three patients?

options.text: IV site redness -> Renal stone pain -> Acute hypoxia
Renal stone pain -> Acute hypoxia -> IV site redness
Acute hypoxia -> Renal stone pain -> IV site redness
Acute hypoxia -> IV site redness -> Renal stone pain

questions.explanation: Acute hypoxia (Breathing/Airway) is always #1. Severe acute physiological pain (8/10) takes priority #2 over mild local IV phlebitis (#3), following ABC, Maslow's physiological tier, and systemic/severe over local/mild.
questions.hint: Rank breathing crisis first, then severe systemic/acute pain, then a minor local IV issue.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: During a mass casualty triage event, a patient has a minor scalp abrasion, is alert, and is walking around helping others. Which START triage color tag should this patient receive?

options.text: Red (Immediate)
Yellow (Delayed)
Green (Minor / Walking wounded)
Black (Expectant)

questions.explanation: In START disaster triage, ambulatory patients with minor injuries ("walking wounded") are directed to a safe area and tagged GREEN (Minor), freeing resources for Red and Yellow casualties.
questions.hint: Recall the triage color designated for "walking wounded" with minor injuries.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A nurse is prioritizing morning care for an elderly patient who has just been extubated 1 hour ago. Which assessment is the HIGHEST priority?

options.text: Checking whether the patient's family brought fresh clothes
Monitoring airway patency, voice quality/stridor, respiratory effort, and SpO2
Performing a complete skin assessment of the heels
Reviewing the patient's lunch menu preferences

questions.explanation: Post-extubation laryngeal edema and airway obstruction are highest risk in the first few hours after removing an endotracheal tube. Continuous Airway and Breathing surveillance is the top priority.
questions.hint: Focus on the immediate complication risk right after an endotracheal tube is removed.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A patient diagnosed with terminal metastatic cancer says quietly, "I don't see the point in continuing chemotherapy anymore." Which response by the nurse is MOST therapeutic?

options.text: "You must stay positive and fight for your family!"
"Don't talk like that; miracles happen every day."
"It sounds like you are feeling exhausted and questioning whether treatment is worth it. Would you like to talk about what matters most to you right now?"
"Why would you quit when the oncologist worked so hard on your plan?"

questions.explanation: Reflecting the patient's emotion and asking an open-ended question validates autonomy and invites meaningful discussion. Options A, B, and D use false reassurance, lecturing, and guilt-inducing "Why?" questioning.
questions.hint: Choose the response that mirrors the patient's feelings without preaching or offering false hope.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: A nurse reviews a new patient's medical chart, reflects on their own personal biases about substance use disorder, and plans the first interview before entering the room. According to Hildegard Peplau, which phase of the therapeutic relationship is occurring?

options.text: Pre-interaction phase
Orientation phase
Working phase
Termination phase

questions.explanation: The pre-interaction phase occurs BEFORE the nurse meets the patient face-to-face. It involves reviewing available data, examining personal feelings/stereotypes, and planning the initial interaction.
questions.hint: Focus on the preparatory phase that takes place before any direct contact with the patient.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: During the working phase of a therapeutic nurse-patient relationship, which nursing activities are MOST characteristic? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Exploring the patient's stressors and helping develop adaptive coping skills
Collaborating with the patient to implement the care plan and evaluate progress
Meeting the patient for the first time and signing the confidentiality contract
Overcoming resistance and supporting behavioral change toward agreed goals

questions.explanation: In Peplau's Working phase, the nurse and patient actively work together to solve problems, build coping mechanisms, address resistance, and evaluate progress. Initial introductions and contract setting happen in the Orientation phase.
questions.hint: Separate active problem-solving and behavioral work from initial introductory tasks.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: A nurse is giving a shift handoff report on a postoperative patient using SBAR. When the nurse says, "I recommend we check a stat hemoglobin and type-and-crossmatch two units of PRBCs," which component of SBAR is being communicated?

options.text: Situation
Background
Assessment
Recommendation

questions.explanation: In SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation), "Recommendation" clearly states the specific action, order, or bedside evaluation the nurse is requesting from the provider.
questions.hint: Identify the SBAR component where the nurse proposes a concrete next step or order.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: A patient with paranoid schizophrenia states, "The ceiling cameras are broadcasting my thoughts to the police!" Which therapeutic communication technique is the nurse using when replying, "I know those thoughts feel very real and frightening to you, but I do not see any cameras broadcasting your thoughts"?

options.text: Challenging and arguing
Reinforcing the delusion
Presenting reality while validating the underlying feeling
Changing the subject abruptly

questions.explanation: Presenting reality states what is real calmly without arguing with or validating a fixed false belief (delusion), while still acknowledging the patient's emotional distress (fear).
questions.hint: Notice how the nurse acknowledges the fear without agreeing with the false belief or arguing aggressively.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: A patient says, "Ever since my heart attack, my whole life is ruined. Nothing works anymore." The nurse responds, "When you say nothing works anymore, could you give me an example of what has been hardest this week?" Which therapeutic technique is demonstrated?

options.text: Giving approval
Seeking clarification / focusing
Belittling feelings
Stereotyping

questions.explanation: Seeking clarification and focusing gently narrow a broad, vague, or overwhelming generalization ("nothing works anymore") into concrete, manageable issues the nurse and patient can address.
questions.hint: Observe how the nurse asks the patient to make a vague sweeping statement more specific.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: A nurse is counseling a patient with newly diagnosed HIV. The patient becomes tearful and stops speaking for 20 seconds. What is the nurse's MOST therapeutic action?

options.text: Fill the silence immediately by talking about medication side effects
Leave the room to give the patient complete privacy without saying anything
Sit quietly beside the patient, maintaining an empathetic, receptive presence until the patient is ready to speak
Tell the patient to stop crying because tears will not help

questions.explanation: Therapeutic silence gives the patient time to process overwhelming emotions, organize thoughts, and feel supported without being rushed or judged.
questions.hint: Remember that purposeful quiet presence can be one of the most powerful therapeutic tools during grief or shock.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: Which of the following statements by a nurse represents the therapeutic technique of "Offering Self"?

options.text: "You should take your blood pressure pills every morning without fail."
"I will sit here with you for a while so you don't have to be alone."
"Why didn't you call the clinic earlier when your chest hurt?"
"Everyone feels nervous before a colonoscopy; you'll get over it."

questions.explanation: Offering self makes the nurse unconditionally available and present to support the patient ("I'll stay with you") without making demands or giving unsolicited advice.
questions.hint: Look for the statement where the nurse offers their supportive presence rather than advice or judgment.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: A patient who had a laryngectomy cannot speak verbally. Which communication strategies should the nurse implement? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Provide a whiteboard, pen, or picture/alphabet communication board
Ensure the patient's call bell is adapted (e.g., light-touch pad) and always within reach
Ask concise questions that can be answered with nods or short written responses
Speak much louder because the patient cannot talk

questions.explanation: Post-laryngectomy patients lose vocal cord phonation, NOT hearing or cognition. Providing writing/picture tools, accessible call bells, and clear short questions ensures safe communication; shouting is inappropriate and demeaning.
questions.hint: Remember that losing the ability to speak does not impair hearing or intelligence.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: A nurse is interviewing a visually impaired patient on admission. Which communication practice is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Touch the patient's arm silently before speaking to get their attention
Announce your presence upon entering the room, identify yourself by name and role, and explain before touching
Speak in a loud voice while standing across the room
Leave the room quietly without telling the patient so you do not disturb them

questions.explanation: With visually impaired patients, always identify yourself verbally upon entering, explain procedures before physical contact to avoid startling them, use a normal tone of voice, and state clearly when you are leaving the room.
questions.hint: Think about how verbal orientation replaces visual cues to keep the patient feeling safe and respected.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: During a discharge teaching session, a nurse notices the patient nodding repeatedly while looking confused and tapping their foot anxiously. Which communication principle is MOST important for the nurse to recognize?

options.text: Verbal nodding always means full comprehension
Non-verbal cues often reveal true feelings or confusion more accurately than verbal agreement
Paralanguage is irrelevant in clinical teaching
The nurse should finish teaching quickly and ignore body language

questions.explanation: Non-verbal communication (facial expressions, fidgeting, posture) is largely unconscious and often more reliable than verbal cues when a patient feels embarrassed to admit they do not understand.
questions.hint: Compare what a patient's polite nod says versus what their anxious body language reveals.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: In the communication process, a nurse uses heavy medical jargon ("Your echocardiogram shows left ventricular ejection fraction reduction with diastolic dysfunction") while speaking to a farmer with primary-school education. What type of communication barrier is this?

options.text: Environmental noise barrier
Semantic (language/jargon) barrier
Physiological hearing barrier
Cultural proxemic barrier

questions.explanation: Semantic barriers occur when words, technical jargon, or abbreviations have different meanings or are incomprehensible to the receiver. Nurses should translate medical concepts into plain, everyday language.
questions.hint: Identify the barrier caused specifically by complex technical vocabulary that the listener cannot decode.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: A nurse says to a patient who just walked down the hallway for the first time after hip replacement, "I noticed you walked all the way to the nurses' station today." Which therapeutic technique is this?

options.text: False reassurance
Giving recognition
Giving personal approval ("I'm so proud of you")
Probing

questions.explanation: Giving recognition objectively acknowledges a patient's effort or achievement without attaching personal value judgments ("good/bad"), fostering internal motivation rather than dependence on the nurse's approval.
questions.hint: Distinguish objective acknowledgment of an effort from subjective praise or approval.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: A psychiatric patient asks the nurse, "Do you think I should divorce my husband?" Which response best upholds therapeutic communication and patient autonomy?

options.text: "Yes, he sounds very stressful for your mental health."
"No, you should try harder to save your marriage."
"That sounds like a very big decision. What are your thoughts and feelings about your relationship right now?"
"I am not allowed to talk about your family."

questions.explanation: Giving personal advice ("Yes/No") robs the patient of autonomy and creates liability. Reflecting the weight of the decision and inviting exploration helps the patient reach their own conclusion.
questions.hint: Avoid taking sides or giving advice; guide the patient to explore their own perspective.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of using "Closed-Ended Questions" appropriately in nursing practice?

options.text: Exploring deep emotional grief during counseling
Gathering rapid, specific factual data during an emergency or focused health history
Encouraging a shy patient to tell their life story
Building long-term psychotherapy insight

questions.explanation: While open-ended questions are best for exploring feelings and broad histories, closed-ended ("Yes/No" or short-fact) questions are essential in emergencies (e.g., "Are you allergic to penicillin?", "Do you have chest pain right now?").
questions.hint: Think about clinical situations where speed and exact factual answers matter more than open storytelling.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: A nurse is ending a 45-minute therapeutic interview with a patient who has been discussing multiple health concerns. Which statement demonstrates the therapeutic technique of "Summarizing"?

options.text: "Tell me more about your childhood."
"Today we discussed your worries about insulin injections, practiced the technique once, and agreed to review your blood sugar log tomorrow."
"Don't worry, everything will be much easier next week."
"Why did you forget your logbook at home?"

questions.explanation: Summarizing reviews the key points discussed during an interaction, reinforces learning, clarifies shared understanding, and provides a smooth transition toward closing the session.
questions.hint: Look for the statement that pulls together the main points covered and confirms the next step.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: Which non-verbal element of communication refers to the tone, pitch, volume, speed, and inflection of a speaker's voice?

options.text: Kinesics
Proxemics
Paralanguage (vocalics)
Haptics

questions.explanation: Paralanguage encompasses vocal qualities beyond the literal words (tone, pitch, rate, volume, sighs). Kinesics = body movement/gestures; Proxemics = personal space; Haptics = touch.
questions.hint: Match vocal qualities like pitch, rate, and tone to the communication term ending in "-language."
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: During a ward round, a junior nurse disagrees with an unclear verbal medication order from a senior resident. Which communication style should the nurse use to advocate safely for the patient?

options.text: Passive communication (staying silent to avoid conflict)
Aggressive communication (shouting at the resident in front of patients)
Assertive communication (calmly, clearly, and respectfully stating the clinical concern using facts/SBAR)
Passive-aggressive communication (ignoring the order without telling anyone)

questions.explanation: Assertive communication expresses clinical concerns clearly, respectfully, and objectively without hostility or submission, protecting patient safety and fostering interprofessional teamwork.
questions.hint: Choose the professional communication style that balances respect with firm advocacy for patient safety.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: A patient with depression says, "I am completely worthless; nobody cares whether I live or die." The nurse replies, "Oh, don't say that! You have a wonderful family and so much to live for." Why is this response NON-THERAPEUTIC?

options.text: It uses therapeutic reflection
It belittles and dismisses the patient's feelings, blocking further expression of potential suicidal ideation
It encourages open-ended exploration
It demonstrates active listening

questions.explanation: Disagreeing with or minimizing a depressed patient's feelings ("Oh, don't say that!") invalidates their pain and can cause them to hide suicidal thoughts. The nurse should validate distress and directly assess suicide safety.
questions.hint: Consider what happens to trust when a nurse contradicts or minimizes a patient's painful emotion.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: Which strategies improve therapeutic communication when caring for a pediatric preschooler (age 3–5 years)? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Get down to the child's eye level to appear less intimidating
Use simple, concrete words and avoid scary idioms (like "put you to sleep" or "take your blood")
Allow the child to touch or play with safe equipment (like a stethoscope) before the exam
Give a detailed 20-minute anatomical lecture before starting any procedure

questions.explanation: Preschoolers are concrete thinkers who take words literally and fear bodily harm. Eye-level posture, concrete non-threatening terms, and medical play reduce fear and build trust.
questions.hint: Think about how preschoolers interpret language literally and respond to physical height and play.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: A nurse is communicating with a patient who has receptive (Wernicke's) aphasia. The patient speaks fluently in long sentences that make no sense and does not understand spoken instructions. Which nursing strategy is MOST helpful?

options.text: Speak faster and use complex multi-step commands
Use short, simple phrases paired with clear gestures, demonstrations, and visual cues in a quiet environment
Ask the patient to write a detailed essay about their symptoms
Shout loudly to overcome the comprehension deficit

questions.explanation: Receptive (Wernicke's) aphasia impairs comprehension of spoken and written language. Pairing simple, concrete words with visual cues and physical demonstration helps convey meaning safely.
questions.hint: Remember that the core deficit here is understanding language, so visual demonstration helps bridge the gap.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: In the nurse-patient relationship, when a patient unconsciously redirects feelings and attitudes originally held toward a parent onto the nurse, this psychological phenomenon is called:

options.text: Countertransference
Transference
Sublimation
Projection of vitals

questions.explanation: Transference occurs when the patient projects feelings from past significant relationships onto the nurse. Countertransference is the reverse—when the nurse unconsciously projects personal feelings onto the patient.
questions.hint: Distinguish when the patient redirects past feelings onto the nurse versus the reverse.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: A nurse notices they feel unusually angry and impatient toward a non-compliant patient because the patient reminds the nurse of their own stubborn uncle. What is this phenomenon, and how should the nurse handle it?

options.text: Transference; avoid caring for the patient without telling anyone
Countertransference; recognize the bias through self-awareness and seek clinical supervision/reflection to maintain objectivity
Empathy; share the personal family story with the patient
Sympathy; lecture the patient firmly

questions.explanation: Countertransference occurs when a nurse's own unresolved feelings/past relationships influence their reaction to a patient. Professional self-awareness and supervision prevent it from harming therapeutic care.
questions.hint: Identify the term for the nurse's own unconscious emotional reaction toward a patient.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Empathy is more effective than sympathy in therapeutic nurse-patient communication.
Reason (R): Empathy allows the nurse to understand the patient's perspective while maintaining professional objectivity, whereas sympathy involves emotional over-involvement that can impair clinical judgment.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.explanation: Empathy is the objective ability to perceive and understand a patient's feelings without losing professional boundaries. Sympathy involves pity or sharing personal emotional distress, which shifts focus away from the patient and clouds judgment.
questions.hint: Contrast objective understanding of another's feelings with emotional over-involvement or pity.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: A nurse conducting a home health visit asks a patient, "What brings you to the clinic today?" or "How have you been managing your breathing at home?" These are examples of:

options.text: Leading questions
Probing questions
Broad openings / open-ended questions
Closed-ended questions

questions.explanation: Broad openings and open-ended questions allow the patient to choose the topic and describe experiences in their own words rather than restricting them to "yes" or "no."
questions.hint: Notice how these questions invite the patient to lead the conversation freely in their own words.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: A nurse is preparing a patient for an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. When the nurse brings the consent form to witness the signature, the patient asks, "Can you explain the possible surgical complications? The doctor rushed out before I could ask." What is the nurse's PRIORITY legal action?

options.text: Explain all surgical risks and complications thoroughly and have the patient sign
Tell the patient to sign anyway because the surgery is already scheduled
Do not obtain the signature; notify the surgeon immediately to return and answer the patient's questions
Ask the patient's spouse to sign on the patient's behalf instead

questions.explanation: Informed consent requires that the performing provider explain risks, benefits, and alternatives BEFORE the patient signs. If the patient has unanswered procedural questions, the nurse must halt the signing and notify the surgeon.
questions.hint: Remember who holds the legal obligation to explain surgical risks before a consent form can be validly signed.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: Which conditions are legally required for an adult's informed consent to be valid? (Select all that apply)

options.text: The patient must be mentally competent (have decision-making capacity)
Consent must be given voluntarily without coercion
Adequate disclosure of procedure, risks, benefits, and alternatives must be provided by the performing provider
The patient must be under preoperative opioid sedation before signing

questions.explanation: Valid informed consent requires competence/capacity, voluntariness, and full disclosure by the provider (with comprehension). Consent signed after receiving sedatives or opioids that impair cognition is legally invalid.
questions.hint: Check the three core legal pillars of valid consent and spot the condition that invalidates capacity.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: A nurse applies bilateral wrist restraints to a mildly restless elderly patient without a physician's order so the nurse can finish charting faster. Which legal torts or violations has the nurse committed? (Select all that apply)

options.text: False imprisonment
Battery (unconsented physical restriction)
Good Samaritan protection
Violation of patient rights and restraint standards

questions.explanation: Restraints may NEVER be used for staff convenience. Applying restraints without clinical justification, failed less-restrictive alternatives, and a proper provider order constitutes false imprisonment, battery, and a serious regulatory violation.
questions.hint: Think about which intentional torts apply when someone is physically tied down without legal or clinical justification.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: A nurse checks a physician's prescription for a newly applied physical restraint on a violently agitated adult patient who was pulling out an endotracheal tube. Which nursing actions are legally and clinically required? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Use a quick-release slip knot tied to the movable bed frame (never the side rails)
Assess circulation, skin integrity, and neurovascular status frequently per policy (e.g., every 15–30 minutes) and release periodically for ROM/toileting
Obtain a PRN ("as needed") standing order for restraints to reuse anytime
Document behavioral justification, less-restrictive measures tried first, and exact times of application and reassessment

questions.explanation: Restraints require a time-limited specific order (PRN restraint orders are strictly prohibited), quick-release knots tied to the bed frame (not side rails, which cause injury when lowered), frequent neurovascular checks, and thorough documentation.
questions.hint: Recall the strict safety rules on knot placement, monitoring, documentation, and whether PRN restraint orders are allowed.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: A nurse discovers that a colleague has been diverting (stealing) IV morphine vials from the ICU narcotics cabinet and appears impaired while on duty. What is the nurse's ethical and legal obligation?

options.text: Ignore the issue to protect the colleague's career
Confront the colleague privately and promise never to tell management
Report the suspected drug diversion and impairment immediately to the nursing supervisor/charge nurse per hospital policy
Post a warning about the colleague in the staff WhatsApp group

questions.explanation: Under the ethical principle of non-maleficence and legal duty to protect patient safety, a nurse must promptly report an impaired colleague through the proper administrative chain of command (supervisor/nursing director).
questions.hint: Prioritize patient safety and follow the formal chain of command rather than covering up or gossiping.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: A 17-year-old unmarried pregnant adolescent arrives at the hospital in active labor and requests pain relief and obstetric care. Who is generally legally authorized to consent for her pregnancy-related medical care?

options.text: Only her school principal
The adolescent herself (under emancipated/mature minor and reproductive healthcare exceptions in most jurisdictions, or legal guardian where required by local statute)
Any hospital security guard
No care can be provided until she turns 18

questions.explanation: Emancipated minors (married, financially independent, armed forces, or legally emancipated) and minors seeking pregnancy/obstetric or emergency care are recognized in medical-legal standards to consent for pregnancy-related care so life-saving maternal-fetal care is never delayed.
questions.hint: Recall the legal exception allowing certain minors (such as emancipated or pregnant minors in labor) to consent to care.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: A nurse accidentally administers penicillin to a patient with a documented severe penicillin allergy, resulting in anaphylactic shock and ICU admission. In a malpractice lawsuit, which element of malpractice is established by proving that the penicillin directly caused the anaphylactic shock?

options.text: Duty of care
Standard of care
Causation (proximate cause)
Informed consent

questions.explanation: In malpractice: Duty = nurse-patient assignment; Breach = failing to check allergies and giving penicillin; Causation = direct link between giving penicillin and the anaphylaxis; Damages = ICU stay/injury.
questions.hint: Match the direct cause-and-effect link between the breach and the injury to one of the four malpractice elements.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: A nurse leaves the bed side rails down and fails to place the call bell within reach for a heavily sedated postoperative patient, who subsequently falls and fractures a hip. This unintentional failure to act as a reasonably prudent nurse would under similar circumstances is legally termed:

options.text: Assault
Libel
Negligence / Malpractice
Fraud

questions.explanation: Negligence is the unintentional failure to exercise the care a reasonably prudent person would; when committed by a licensed professional failing to meet professional nursing standards, it is malpractice (professional negligence).
questions.hint: Distinguish unintentional failure to meet safety standards from intentional torts like assault or defamation.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: Under the legal doctrine of "Respondeat Superior," who may be held vicariously liable along with the nurse if a nurse commits negligence while acting within the scope of employment?

options.text: The patient's family
The employing hospital or healthcare institution
The Indian Nursing Council only
The patient's health insurance company

questions.explanation: "Respondeat superior" ("let the master answer") holds an employer (hospital) vicariously liable for negligent acts committed by employees within the scope of their employment—though the individual nurse always remains personally accountable too.
questions.hint: Translate the Latin phrase "let the master answer" to identify who shares liability with the employee.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: A surgical sponge is accidentally left inside a patient's abdomen after surgery, and the injury clearly could not have occurred without negligence by the surgical team. Which legal doctrine shifts the burden of proof to the defendants because "the thing speaks for itself"?

options.text: Good Samaritan doctrine
Res ipsa loquitur
Stare decisis
Habeas corpus

questions.explanation: "Res ipsa loquitur" ("the thing speaks for itself") applies when an injury (such as a retained surgical instrument/sponge) is of a kind that ordinarily does not happen without negligence and was under the exclusive control of the defendants.
questions.hint: Recall the Latin legal phrase meaning "the thing speaks for itself."
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: A terminally ill patient with full decision-making capacity has executed a written legal document specifying that they do not want mechanical ventilation or tube feeding if they become unable to communicate. What is this document called?

options.text: Incident report
Living will (a type of Advance Directive)
Informed surgical consent
AMA form

questions.explanation: A Living Will is an advance directive detailing the specific medical treatments a person does or does not want in end-of-life situations if they lose capacity. A Durable Power of Attorney for Healthcare designates a surrogate decision-maker.
questions.hint: Identify the specific advance directive that states treatment preferences in writing before incapacity occurs.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: A patient has a valid, physician-signed "Do Not Resuscitate" (DNR) order in the medical chart. Which nursing action is APPROPRIATE for this patient?

options.text: Discontinue all pain medications, oxygen, and hygiene care
Continue all comfort care, pain management, hygiene, and prescribed treatments, while withholding CPR/defibrillation if cardiopulmonary arrest occurs
Refuse to check the patient's vital signs
Perform full CPR anyway if a family member panics at the bedside

questions.explanation: A DNR order means ONLY that cardiopulmonary resuscitation (compressions, intubation, defibrillation) is withheld upon arrest. All other comfort, palliative, pain relief, and dignified nursing care MUST continue.
questions.hint: Clarify that DNR withholds resuscitation during arrest—it never means "do not treat" or "do not comfort."
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a 5-year-old child brought to the emergency room with multiple bruises in different stages of healing, cigarette burn marks, and an inconsistent caregiver story. What is the nurse's LEGAL responsibility?

options.text: Confront the parents aggressively and accuse them of abuse
Promise the parents confidentiality if they admit what happened
Report the suspected child abuse immediately to the appropriate legal/child protective authorities and physician as a mandated reporter
Ignore the findings unless the child explicitly asks for police

questions.explanation: Nurses are legally mandated reporters of suspected child abuse, elder abuse, domestic violence (per jurisdiction), and medico-legal cases (MLC). Reporting requires only reasonable suspicion, not absolute proof.
questions.hint: Recall a nurse's statutory duty as a mandated reporter when non-accidental trauma is suspected.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: While caring for an inpatient, a nurse hears a colleague loudly gossiping in the hospital cafeteria about a celebrity patient's psychiatric diagnosis and HIV status. Which ethical principle and legal right is the colleague violating?

options.text: Fidelity and Good Samaritan law
Confidentiality and the patient's legal right to privacy
Veracity and Res ipsa loquitur
Justice and Respondeat superior

questions.explanation: Discussing identifiable patient health information in public areas (cafeterias, elevators, social media) breaches ethical confidentiality and legal privacy protections (e.g., HIPAA / Indian clinical privacy standards).
questions.hint: Identify the core duty violated whenever private patient health information is discussed in public spaces.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: A nurse realizes they made a documentation error in a paper nursing progress note after writing the wrong blood pressure value. What is the LEGALLY correct way to correct this entry?

options.text: Use correction fluid (whitener) to cover the mistake completely
Tear out the entire page and rewrite the shift notes
Draw a single straight line through the error, write "error" (or "mistaken entry"), initial/date/time it, and write the correct entry
Scribble heavily over the wrong numbers so nobody can read them

questions.explanation: Because a medical record is a legal document, obliterating, erasing, using correction fluid, or tearing out pages suggests tampering/fraud in court. A single line through the error with initials, date, and accurate entry preserves audit integrity.
questions.hint: Think about how to correct a legal record transparently without making it look like tampering.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: Which of the following is the primary ethical focus of the principle of "Non-maleficence"?

options.text: Telling the truth at all times
"First, do no harm" (preventing intentional or unintentional harm to patients)
Distributing organs fairly on a transplant list
Keeping promises made to colleagues

questions.explanation: Non-maleficence (*primum non nocere*) obligates nurses to avoid causing harm—for example, checking the Rights of Medication Administration, raising fall precautions, and questioning unsafe orders.
questions.hint: Translate the classic bioethical maxim *primum non nocere*.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: A nurse tells a colleague verbally in the breakroom, "Nurse Priya failed her nursing exam three times and falsifies patient charts," knowing this is completely false, which causes Nurse Priya to lose a promotion. Which intentional tort has been committed?

options.text: Libel
Slander
Battery
False imprisonment

questions.explanation: Slander is spoken (oral) defamation of character that harms another person's reputation. Libel is written or published defamation.
questions.hint: Distinguish between spoken defamation and written defamation by matching the first letter of "Spoken."
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: Which of the following situations qualify as an ethical dilemma in nursing practice?

options.text: Choosing which color pen to use for shift notes
A terminally ill patient's family demands that the nurse hide a cancer diagnosis from the alert, competent patient who is directly asking for the truth
Calculating an IV drip rate using a standard formula
Performing hand hygiene before inserting a Foley catheter

questions.explanation: An ethical dilemma occurs when two or more ethical principles conflict with no easy solution—here, Veracity and Autonomy (the competent patient's right to know) conflict with family wishes and perceived Beneficence/cultural protection.
questions.hint: Look for a scenario where two competing moral principles directly clash.
